title: Q5.1: Classification of Salivary Gland Tumours, Pleomorphic Adenoma & Parotidectomy

children.title: Covers: KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 17, RGU, TU — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers
80% of salivary gland neoplasms arise in the major glands, and ~80% of these occur in the Parotid gland
80% of parotid tumours are benign, and 80% of benign parotid tumours are Pleomorphic Adenomas
Smaller the salivary gland, higher the likelihood of malignancy
2. WHO Classification of Salivary Gland Neoplasms (Table 54.3)
Warthin’s tumour (Adenolymphoma / Papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum — second commonest benign tumour)
Low-grade Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (commonest salivary malignancy overall and in children)
Adenoid cystic carcinoma (propensity for perineural invasion and “Swiss-cheese” cribriform histology)
Non-Hodgkin’s MALT lymphoma (associated with Sjögren’s syndrome)
Peaks in the 3rd to 5th decades (average age 45 years)
>80% occur in the parotid (mostly in the superficial lobe / tail of parotid)
Well-circumscribed, firm, lobulated/bosselated mass with a whitish-tan, cartilaginous cut surface
Fibrous capsule is incomplete and has microscopic pseudopods (finger-like extensions) projecting into the surrounding normal gland parenchyma
It leaves behind pseudopods, leading to multifocal recurrence
Biphasic admixture of epithelial and myoepithelial cells (ducts, sheets, strands) embedded in a mesenchymal-like stroma (myxoid, mucoid, chondroid/cartilaginous, and hyalinised matrix)
Myoepithelial cells express p63, S-100, and SMA
Slow-growing, painless, firm-to-cartilaginous swelling in the parotid region (in front of and below the ear lobule, obliterating the retromandibular groove and lifting the ear lobule)
Freely mobile over deeper structures (becomes less mobile when the masseter is contracted)
Facial nerve is completely intact (0% palsy in benign lesions)
May pass through the stylomandibular tunnel (“dumbbell tumour”) to present as a medial paratonsillar / soft palate bulge pushing the tonsil medially
Clinical Features Suggestive of Malignant Transformation (Carcinoma ex Pleomorphic Adenoma)
Sudden rapid increase in size of a longstanding swelling
Shows a well-defined, lobulated hypoechoic mass with posterior acoustic enhancement
Reported using the Milan System (Categories I–VI; Pleomorphic adenoma = Category IVA)
Core biopsy is reserved for inconclusive cases or suspected lymphoma
Open incisional biopsy is contraindicated due to tumour seeding
Indicated for large tumours (>4 cm), suspected deep lobe involvement, recurrent tumours, or suspected malignancy
Excision of the tumour with a cuff of normal surrounding parotid tissue while preserving the facial nerve
Superficial Parotidectomy (or Adequate Parotidectomy / Extracapsular Dissection in select mobile tail lesions)
For tumours lateral to the facial nerve plane (Patey’s faciovenous plane)
Excising both superficial and deep lobes while preserving the facial nerve
Sacrificing the facial nerve with immediate cable nerve grafting using the great auricular nerve or sural nerve, plus neck dissection and adjuvant radiotherapy
Lazy-S (Modified Blair) incision (preauricular crease, curving around the ear lobule over the mastoid, and running forward in a neck crease two finger-breadths below the angle of the mandible)
Raise an anterior skin flap in the subplatysmal / sub-SMAS plane
Divide the anterior branch of the great auricular nerve while preserving its posterior branch if possible
Anatomical Landmarks to Identify the Facial Nerve Trunk (Antegrade Technique)
Facial nerve trunk lies 1 cm deep and 1 cm inferior to the cartilaginous tip of the tragus
Nerve lies just superior to the upper border of the posterior digastric near its mastoid insertion
Nerve lies 6–8 mm deep/inferior to the drop-off of this bony suture line (most constant landmark)
Nerve lies superficial to its base
Tracing peripheral branches — e.g., buccal branch parallel to Stensen’s duct or marginal mandibular branch crossing facial vessels — proximally to the trunk
Dissect in Patey’s faciovenous plane immediately superficial to the facial nerve branches using fine mosquito forceps and bipolar cautery up to Stensen’s duct, which is ligated
Place a suction drain and close in layers
Temporary facial nerve paresis (neuropraxia; commonest in the marginal mandibular branch)
Permanent facial nerve palsy (requires eye care to prevent exposure keratitis)
Numbness of the ear lobule (due to division of the great auricular nerve — C2, C3)
Second most common benign salivary gland tumour (5–15% of parotid neoplasms)
Occurs almost exclusively in the Parotid gland (typically in the lower pole / tail)
Strongly associated with cigarette smoking (8-fold higher risk)
Affects older men in their 6th to 7th decades (male:female historically predominance, now equalising with smoking trends)
10% are bilateral and 10% are multifocal (synchronous or metachronous)
Thought to arise from heterotopic salivary ductal inclusions trapped within intraparotid lymph nodes during late embryological encapsulation of the parotid
Cut surface shows cystic spaces filled with murky, chocolate-brown mucoid fluid (“motor-oil fluid”)

Papillary and cystic structures lined by a characteristic double layer of eosinophilic oncocytic epithelial cells (rich in mitochondria) resting on a dense reactive lymphoid stroma with germinal centres
On Technetium-99m ((99m)Tc) pertechnetate scintigraphy, Warthin’s tumour is uniquely “Hot” (concentrates radioisotope due to high mitochondrial content in oncocytic cells)

Following parotidectomy or parotid trauma, severed postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres undergo aberrant regeneration and cross-innervate the sympathetic-innervated dermal sweat glands and cutaneous blood vessels of the overlying skin flap
Inferior salivatory nucleus → Glossopharyngeal nerve [CN IX] → Jacobson’s nerve → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve
Both parasympathetic secretomotor fibres and sympathetic fibres use acetylcholine as their neurotransmitter
Eating or thinking of food (salivary stimulus) triggers inappropriate sweating, flushing, erythema, and warmth over the preauricular/cheek skin in the distribution of the auriculotemporal nerve
Paint the affected preauricular skin with iodine solution, allow it to dry, dust with dry white starch powder, and give the patient a sialogogue (lemon slice)
Sweating dissolves the iodine to react with starch, turning the affected skin dark blue-black
Raise a thick skin flap (preserving SMAS)
Or interpose a physical barrier between the parotid bed and skin (e.g., sternocleidomastoid muscle flap, temporalis fascia flap, acellular dermal matrix [Alloderm], or autologous fat graft)
Management of Established Frey’s Syndrome (Summary Box 54.9)
Intradermal Botulinum Toxin A injections into the affected skin (gold standard)
Blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuroglandular junction
Tympanic Neurectomy (division of Jacobson’s nerve on the promontory of the middle ear) for refractory cases

title: Q5.3: Ranula, Submandibular Sialolithiasis & Stafne Bone Cyst

children.title: A mucous extravasation retention cyst of the floor of the mouth arising from rupture or obstruction of the ducts (ducts of Rivinus / Bartholin’s duct) or acini of the sublingual salivary gland

Presents in children/young adults as a unilateral, painless, soft, fluctuant, translucent bluish swelling in the anterior floor of the mouth lateral to the frenulum, resembling a frog’s belly (Latin: rana = frog)
The mucus collection herniates/insinuates through a dehiscence in the mylohyoid muscle (or around its posterior free border) into the submandibular/submental space
Presenting as a painless neck swelling with or without an intraoral component (bidigitally palpable)
MRI or USG confirms a cystic lesion with a “tail sign” extending into the sublingual space
Aspiration yields thick, viscid, mucinous saliva with high amylase (distinguishing it from a lymphatic malformation/cystic hygroma or dermoid cyst)
Excision of the ipsilateral Sublingual Gland along with decompression/evacuation of the cyst via a transoral approach (definitive cure)
Simple incision/drainage or marsupialisation has a high recurrence rate because the sublingual gland has multiple autonomous ducts
Non-surgical alternatives: Intralesional injection of sclerosant OK-432 (Picibanil) or Botulinum toxin
85% of all salivary calculi occur in the submandibular gland/Wharton’s duct (vs 15% in the parotid)
Submandibular secretion is rich in mucin, calcium, and phosphate, making it more viscous and alkaline
Wharton’s duct is long, tortuous, and has an antigravity ascending course with a narrow orifice (punctum), predisposing to salivary stasis
Acute, colicky pain and rapid tense swelling of the submandibular gland just before or during meals (especially sour foods)
Slowly subsides over 1–2 hours after eating
Reduced saliva from the inflamed sublingual papilla
Stone is palpable on bidigital palpation of the floor of the mouth (palpating from posterior to anterior)
80% of submandibular stones are radio-opaque (composed of calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate)
High-Resolution Ultrasonography or non-contrast CT (detects radiolucent and small stones with acoustic shadowing)
Hydration, sialogogues, gland massage, and antibiotics if infected
Larger (>5 mm) impacted stones in the floor of the mouth: Transoral Choanal Duct Slitting (Sialolithotomy)
Place a stay suture behind the stone to prevent it from slipping back into the hilum
Incise the longitudinal axis of Wharton’s duct directly over the stone
Leave the duct open or marsupialise (never suture the duct closed as it causes stricture)
Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL for stones <7 mm)
Submandibular Gland Excision (preserving the marginal mandibular nerve, lingual nerve, and hypoglossal nerve)
3. Stafne Bone Cyst (Static Bone Cavity of Mandible) [KU 18]
A developmental pseudocystic depression on the lingual cortex of the mandible containing ectopic/entrapped submandibular salivary gland tissue and branches of the facial artery
A well-corticated, round, unilocular radiolucency (0.5–2 cm) located in the posterior mandible below the inferior alveolar nerve canal between the first molar and the angle of the mandible
Requires reassurance and no surgical intervention
The thyroid gland develops from the median endodermal bud at the foramen caecum of the tongue and descends caudally in front of the pharynx as the hollow thyroglossal duct
The duct passes in intimate continuity with (anterior, through, or posterior to) the body of the developing hyoid bone before reaching its final position in the lower neck
The duct normally obliterates by the 6th–8th week
Persistence of an unobliterated segment forms a Thyroglossal Cyst
Subhyoid / Infrahyoid (60–75% — Commonest): Between the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage
Over the thyroid cartilage (often slightly to the left of the midline)
Floor of the mouth / Intralingual (Foramen caecum)
Presents most commonly in children and young adults as a painless, smooth, cystic midline neck swelling
Moves upwards on protrusion of the tongue (Tugging Sign)
Because the cyst remains tethered to the base of the tongue (foramen caecum) via the patent thyroglossal tract passing through the hyoid bone
Holding the cyst between thumb and index finger while asking the patient to protrude the tongue elicits a distinct upward tug
Recurrent Infection & Abscess Formation (due to lymphoid tissue in its wall)
Never congenital; always acquired following spontaneous rupture or inadequate surgical incision/drainage of an infected thyroglossal cyst
Presents as a midline pinpoint opening below the hyoid, discharging mucus/pus
Covered by a characteristic crescentic hood of skin (“hood sign”) superiorly that is pulled inwards on tongue protrusion
Almost always Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma arising in ectopic thyroid tissue within the cyst wall
Confirms the cystic nature of the swelling
Verifies the presence of a normal orthotopic thyroid gland in the lower neck (mandatory before excision, lest the cyst contains the patient’s only functioning thyroid tissue)
Thyroid Function Tests (TSH, Free T4) and FNAC (if a solid mural nodule is seen)
Excision of the cyst alone has a >40% recurrence rate because microscopic epithelial ductules pass through the hyoid bone up to the foramen caecum
Components of Sistrunk’s Operation: Complete en bloc excision of
The thyroglossal cyst (and fistulous tract with an ellipse of skin, if a fistula is present)
The central segment (body) of the hyoid bone (1–1.5 cm between the lesser cornua)
A core of suprahyoid muscle tissue (mylohyoid, geniohyoid, genioglossus) along the entire embryonic tract up to the foramen caecum
